name: The Monorchid
label: Touch and Go
lede: Two Circus Lupus veterans got back together, made a run of singles and one LP for small labels, and broke up before Touch and Go released the second album. The sleeve says so: R.I.P. May 1995 to Sept. 1997.

eras.title: After Circus Lupus
eras.text: When Circus Lupus split in 1993, singer Chris Thomson and guitarist Chris Hamley went separate ways. Two years later they were back in the same band, with three more D.C. lifers.

years.src: Trouser Press: Circus Lupus · Portland Show-Guide
years.h: Circus Lupus splits, and Thomson starts [[Las Mordidas|6e471c60-ce00-4d4e-a2af-b61fa6e95574]]
years.p: Trouser Press calls the new band a one-single groove-punk quartet. The Portland Show-Guide says it turned into the Monorchid through line-up changes.

years.src: Discogs: Monorchid · Trouser Press: Circus Lupus · DCist
years.h: Thomson and Hamley reunite, with Cone, Coronado and Allnutt
years.p: Andy Cone joins Hamley on guitar over Andy Coronado's bass and Tom Allnutt's drums. Discogs notes some people called the sound "cajuncore."
years.xp: Thomson, who'd played bass in [[Ignition|3cb2b7d6-1f0b-4ac5-b67f-52132f3d3b61]] before singing in Circus Lupus, is the voice. Trouser Press says the band still circled the spastic-rock axis but leaned harder on the rock side, with the two guitars drawing "audio Spirograph" patterns over a tight rhythm section.

eras.title: Lovitt's first record, J. Robbins' Inner Ear
eras.text: The Monorchid made its name on 7-inches for small labels, then cut one album at Inner Ear with Jawbox's J. Robbins. By the fall of 1997 it was over.

years.h: Impostor Costume is Lovitt Records' first release
years.p: The debut single starts a run of 7-inches: a track on the Lovitt Empire comp, then singles on San Diego's Gravity Records and on Simple Machines.

years.src: Lovitt Records · DCist · Portland Show-Guide · Discogs: Let Them Eat
yt: Bitch Test, live at the Velvet Elvis, Seattle, 1997
years.h: J. Robbins records Let Them Eat... at Inner Ear
years.p: Simple Machines and Dischord put out the CD and Lovitt the vinyl. Lovitt says Alternative Press later ranked it No. 89 among the best albums of the '90s.
years.xp:
[[J. Robbins|3babd931-a940-43a8-b629-d7aed5b821d9]] of [[Jawbox|016fba14-1fc6-4986-86c2-2113ec9b28de]] recorded it at Inner Ear in late 1996. Its working title, per Lovitt, was Hypodermic Iglesias. Also on it: Midget Housing and Dead Signal.

DCist later described Hamley's and Cone's guitars as locked in "an endless sudden-death knife fight" under Thomson's sneer.

years.src: Discogs: Who Put Out the Fire? · Trouser Press: Circus Lupus
years.h: Last songs on 8-track at Pirate House, then R.I.P.
years.p: Juan Carrera records most of the second album on eight tracks at Pirate House in D.C. in September 1997. That same month the band ends, after Hamley and Cone leave.
years.xp: Three songs, Skin Problems, A.P.B. and What We Need Is More Than This, were already done: Chuck Scott recorded them that January at Knee Deep in Tenafly, New Jersey.

eras.title: A record from a band that's gone
eras.text: Touch and Go put out the album nine months after the band ended. It's 25 minutes long.

years.src: Discogs: Who Put Out the Fire? · Bandcamp: The Monorchid · The A.V. Club · Portland Show-Guide · Soft Riot
years.h: Touch and Go releases Who Put Out the Fire?
years.p: Eleven songs, none past three minutes, with "The Monorchid R.I.P. May 1995 – Sept. 1997" printed in the notes. Cover art is credited to Eddie Janney, photos to Toby Morris.
years.xp:
The A.V. Club called it "a great album, and a great tombstone for The Monorchid," comparing Thomson's delivery to Mark E. Smith and the guitars to Gang of Four. The Portland Show-Guide says many consider it the band's peak.

Afterward Thomson and Coronado played together in [[Skull Kontrol|0e327a14-3b74-4635-a9fa-b9060b3acd13]], and Thomson went on to the Red-Eyed Legends and Coffin Pricks. Soft Riot remembers Coronado touring with Glass Candy around 2001 and 2002.

eras.title: One more set, at the Hideout
eras.text: For Touch and Go's 25th birthday the label brought back bands from every era of its catalog. The Monorchid came back for one afternoon.

years.cap: The Monorchid at Touch and Go's 25th anniversary, Hideout Block Party, Chicago, September 2006
years.src: Setlist.fm · Oh My Rockness · Discogs: Monorchid
yt: Monorchid at Touch and Go's 25th anniversary
years.h: The Monorchid reunite for Touch and Go's 25th birthday
years.p: They play a 2 p.m. set at the Hideout Block Party in Chicago, on a bill with [[Calexico|5e372a49-5672-4fb8-ba14-18c90780c4f9]], [[Seam|24d2e33e-6493-49c9-a5b1-fc82eb2f7d4d]], [[Arcwelder|b1b5e551-95bb-4cff-b740-0c6fa11c66e3]], [[Quasi|3df29542-402a-49a5-ae1f-82f936184b3b]] and [[CocoRosie|e162b2eb-6a42-4240-8c1b-c94d9a0acb73]].
years.xp: The Hideout Block Party was in its tenth year; Touch and Go took it over for the anniversary weekend. Two fan-shot videos of the Monorchid set are on YouTube.

q: We were odd balls. We were kind of doing our own thing.
years.h: DCist puts Let Them Eat... in its Secret History
years.p: Looking back, Thomson told DCist the band grew up inside the D.C. scene and fit in, and didn't.
